metadata.title: Science and mathematics preservice teachers’ perceptions and experiences of practicing dialogic teaching in generative AI-powered virtual reality simulation

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study does not use TIMSS/PISA-style student microdata for achievement scoring; instead, it uses a purposive sample of 34 preservice secondary teachers who participated in a 2-hour EVETeach simulation session. Because the dependent variables are qualitative perceptions/experiences and coded dialogic talk-move frequencies, there is no complex survey sampling frame and no ILSA design weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) to apply. The only mention of TIMSS is as a source of classroom recordings used to localize/train the AI-powered virtual students, not as an analyzed assessment dataset with PV-based outcomes. Therefore, weighting is not part of the analytic strategy; the analysis relies on inductive thematic coding and interrater reliability rather than weighted estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values are not applicable because the study does not model cognitive achievement outcomes from an ILSA assessment (e.g., TIMSS/PISA PV-based math/science scores). The outcomes are preservice teachers’ perceptions/experiences collected via interviews, field notes, and dialogue logs, and the analysis is qualitative thematic coding plus descriptive counts of coded talk moves. Missing-data handling is not reported because the study does not describe an imputation/deletion procedure for PV-based quantitative variables; instead, it reports coding coverage and interrater reliability for the qualitative dataset.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Purposive sample of 34 preservice secondary teachers recruited from multiple teacher education programs at a large research university in the Southeastern U.S. Inclusion criteria: (1) preservice teachers in science and mathematics-related areas, (2) currently enrolled in teacher preparation programs, (3) over 18 years old. Additional participant composition details are reported (e.g., subject focus: Biology/Math/Science/STEM education; teaching-related experience <2 years, >2 years, or none). The study does not report any country-level or assessment-score-based filtering because it is not analyzing an ILSA student assessment dataset; it analyzes participants’ interactions within the EVETeach simulation.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This qualitative multi-case study examines science and mathematics preservice teachers’ perceptions and experiences of practicing dialogic teaching with generative AI-powered virtual students in the EVETeach virtual reality simulation. The study uses a purposive sample of 34 preservice secondary teachers (U.S.-based) who completed a 2-hour Zoom session with text-based interaction, followed by semi-structured interviews; data sources included recorded videos, field notes, dialogue logs, and interviews. Analysis employed inductive thematic coding with within-case thematic analysis and cross-case comparisons, reporting interrater reliability (Cohen’s kappa κ = 0.82) and 100% interrater agreement after peer debriefing. Results are reported as four qualitative themes (engagement dynamics; authenticity/variances; pedagogical sandbox; supplement to teacher preparation) and descriptive frequencies of dialogic talk moves (e.g., open-ended questions n = 509; dialogic talk moves overall n = 1,274). Limitations include the qualitative design (findings as trends), subject-area specificity (science/math), and that the think-aloud protocol may affect perceived realism. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse for ILSA/ML-specific fields because the paper is not an empirical predictive ML study on TIMSS/PISA achievement outcomes. It does not train or evaluate predictive models on assessment data; instead, it uses qualitative thematic analysis of preservice teachers’ experiences and coded dialogic talk moves. Although TIMSS is mentioned as a source of classroom recordings to localize/train the virtual students, the study does not analyze TIMSS student achievement PVs, does not report PV handling, and does not provide ML performance metrics.
